pr_title: Bluetooth: Host: Fix wrong ID being stored
pr_comments: Another request: These commits first add the test and then the fix. It would be much nicer to do it in the opposite order so main is kept bisectable.

> Another request: These commits first add the test and then the fix. It would be much nicer to do it in the opposite order so main is kept bisectable.

Isn't it correct that bisecting will find a failure at the commit before the fix? After all, the bug *did exist* on master. I don't agree that this breaks bisecting. When bisecting, you specify a 'good' commit at which point the test is passing. In most cases this will be the latest commit on master that passed the particular test you are interested in according to CI.

The benefit of adding the test first is that it's super easy to 'checkout' the test before the fix and verify that it fails. I like that.

> Isn't it correct that bisecting will find a failure at the commit before the fix? After all, the bug did exist on master. I don't agree that this breaks bisecting.

When bisecting you are searching for the origin of a currently existing bug, and trying to find when it was introduced. You don't want to have spurious failures due to bugs which were fixed pop up in the middle of the bisect.

> > Isn't it correct that bisecting will find a failure at the commit before the fix? After all, the bug did exist on master. I don't agree that this breaks bisecting.
> 
> When bisecting you are searching for the origin of a currently existing bug, and trying to find when it was introduced. You don't want to have spurious failures due to bugs which were fixed pop up in the middle of the bisect.

This answer ignores most of my comment. I think there is a real convenience to be had for those who want to do TDD. And I can't think of a realistic scenario of bisect failing due if the test is added before the fix. It simply does not matter; Realistically, you don't bisect using the entire test suite (since that takes several hours to run). You bisect with some specific test that had a regression from passing to failing.

issue_context.title: Bluetooth: Host: ID: bt_id_create API fails to store the created identity in Settings under certain conditions
comments: This issue has been marked as stale because it has been open (more than) 60 days with no activity. Remove the stale label or add a comment saying that you would like to have the label removed otherwise this issue will automatically be closed in 14 days. Note, that you can always re-open a closed issue at any time.
This is a high-priority bug because it can make all the settings associated with a particular identity disappear, and not be loaded after boot.

review_comments: So `id_create()` calls a function that uses `bt_dev.id_count` instead of `new_id` @theob-pro ?

`id_create()` will call `bt_settings_save_id()`, which will use the number of identity (`bt_dev.id_count`) to store the settings. `new_id` is the value of the new ID we want to create, the value is `bt_dev.id_count` before the creation of this new ID.
So it's not an error that `bt_settings_save_id()` use `bt_dev.id_count` instead of `new_id`.

@carlescufi I explained it to myself like this: `id_create` takes a specific `new_id`. It is the responsibility of the caller to allocate an id number. `bt_dev.id_count++` is the allocation. `bt_dev.id_count--` is the corresponding de-allocation.

I, too, found it a bit confusing. For future work / not in this PR: I think we should add helper functions for the allocation and de-allocation. Especially since it's possible to delete an id with a number between other ids, so the id namespace becomes fragmented. This is not handled optimally in the code here.
